## Week 5: what structures can we model?

The methods, introduced together and compared under one protocol. Ridge and lasso: what a penalty changes, what $\lambda$ controls, fitting when $p > n$. Additive models: a spline as regression on basis functions, one curve per input, the basis size as the knob. Trees and forests: how a small tree predicts, why it is unstable, what averaging does. Then one simulated dataset for each kind of truth (sparse linear, additive smooth, thresholds with an interaction), every family fitted to each, and the four dimensions on which a method bets: wide or tall, sparse or dense, smooth or discontinuous, additive or interactive. Training error flatters every one of them (the optimism theorem, stated; its proof is yours before the seminar). The three-way split, training, selection and a test set opened once, is used from the first slide.

**Reading**

- ISLR Chapter 6 (Linear Model Selection and Regularization), sections 6.2.1–6.2.2, pp. 237–250: ridge regression and the lasso, and what each penalty does to the coefficients. Stop before 6.2.3; choosing $\lambda$ by cross-validation is week 7.
- ISLR Chapter 7 (Moving Beyond Linearity), sections 7.3–7.4, pp. 294–301 (basis functions and regression splines), and section 7.7, pp. 306–310 (generalized additive models; 7.7.1 fits one by least squares on spline basis functions, as the lecture does, and the GAM part of the lab in 7.8 has the `lm` and `ns()` code). Section 7.5, smoothing splines, is week 7. Skim 7.6, pp. 304–306: local regression is named in the lecture and not examined.
- ISLR Chapter 8 (Tree-Based Methods), section 8.1.1, pp. 328–335 (regression trees), and sections 8.2.1–8.2.2, pp. 340–345 (bagging and random forests). Skim 8.1.2–8.1.4, pp. 335–340. Section 8.2.3, boosting, is week 8.

Optional: PPA Chapter 6 (Generalization), "Generalization gap", pp. 100–101, the setting of the optimism theorem.

**Lecture and seminar:** released here at the start of the week. All three families and the baselines on one dataset, one leaderboard, the three-way split enforced. Data: Spotify tracks (what makes a song popular; a data note comes with the notebook), the penguins, the movies, simulated data.
